name: Reliability and Resilience Interview Prep
description: 20 advanced questions on graceful degradation, retries, timeouts, bulkheads, incident response, and failure-domain design.

cards.front: 1. What is the difference between reliability and resilience?
cards.back: Reliability is about the system staying correct and available under normal and abnormal conditions, while resilience is about how well it recovers from failure. A resilient system degrades and restores gracefully.

cards.front: 2. Why are timeouts mandatory in distributed systems?
cards.back: Without timeouts, callers can wait forever on a broken dependency and tie up resources. Timeouts turn silent hangs into explicit failure paths.

cards.front: 3. What is the danger of retries?
cards.back: Retries can magnify load, duplicate side effects, and create retry storms during incidents. They need limits, jitter, and a clear idempotency story.

cards.front: 4. What does a circuit breaker actually protect?
cards.back: It protects the system from repeatedly calling a failing dependency and wasting resources on hopeless requests. It trades short-term rejection for long-term stability.

cards.front: 5. How do bulkheads improve resilience?
cards.back: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one failure cannot exhaust the entire system. They are the difference between a contained incident and a cascading outage.

cards.front: 6. What is graceful degradation?
cards.back: Graceful degradation means the system continues to provide reduced but useful functionality when a dependency or capacity limit is hit. It is better than total failure because it preserves the user journey.

cards.front: 7. What is the role of idempotency in resilience?
cards.back: Idempotency makes retries safe and lets the system recover from uncertain network outcomes without duplicating work. It is one of the most important tools for stable recovery.

cards.front: 8. How do you choose between fail-open and fail-closed behavior?
cards.back: Fail-open preserves availability but may weaken correctness or security, while fail-closed protects correctness or safety at the cost of availability. The choice depends on the business risk of the failure.

cards.front: 9. Why are SLOs and error budgets part of reliability design?
cards.back: They turn reliability into an explicit product contract instead of a vague hope. Error budgets also tell teams when to slow feature work and pay down operational debt.

cards.front: 10. What makes a good fallback path?
cards.back: A good fallback is cheaper, simpler, and known to work under stress, even if it provides reduced functionality. If the fallback is not tested, it is not a real fallback.

cards.front: 11. How do you design for partial outages?
cards.back: Assume some regions, dependencies, or pods fail while the rest of the system keeps running. The design should route around the failure and preserve the highest-priority user flows.

cards.front: 12. Why are incident runbooks important?
cards.back: Runbooks reduce decision-making time during high-pressure events and make recovery more repeatable. They also expose gaps in monitoring and operational ownership.

cards.front: 13. What is the right way to think about chaos testing?
cards.back: Chaos testing deliberately exercises failure paths so you learn whether the system really degrades as designed. It is valuable when it validates assumptions, not when it creates uncontrolled noise.

cards.front: 14. What causes cascading failures?
cards.back: Usually a combination of retries, shared dependencies, saturated resources, and poor isolation. Cascades happen when one failure turns into a load multiplier for the rest of the system.

cards.front: 15. How do you think about capacity headroom?
cards.back: Headroom is the buffer that keeps the system stable during spikes, failure of a node, or partial degradation. A system with no headroom is one incident away from collapse.

cards.front: 16. Why does observability matter for resilience?
cards.back: Because you cannot safely recover from what you cannot see. Metrics, logs, traces, and alerts tell you whether mitigation is working or just hiding the problem.

cards.front: 17. How should you handle a dependency outage?
cards.back: Stop hammering the dependency, degrade or shed work, and move traffic to a safe fallback if one exists. The goal is to protect the rest of the system while the dependency recovers.

cards.front: 18. What is the difference between availability and recoverability?
cards.back: Availability is the ability to serve requests now; recoverability is how quickly the system can return to healthy operation after failure. Both matter, but they are not the same metric.

cards.front: 19. What should postmortems change?
cards.back: They should change systems, runbooks, alerting, ownership, or design assumptions, not just document the incident. If nothing changes, the postmortem was just paperwork.

cards.front: 20. When is resilience engineering overkill?
cards.back: It is overkill for low-value, low-criticality flows that can tolerate simple retries or occasional failure. The investment should match the business impact of an outage.

author: Gemini
